entities.summary:
Jean-Baptiste Alliette, known by his pseudonym Etteilla, revolutionized the practice of cartomancy in late 18th-century France, specifically through his systematic reinterpretation of the Tarot de Marseille. Born in Paris around 1738 and dying there on December 12, 1791, Etteilla was the first to publish a comprehensive system for divinatory tarot, thereby professionalizing and popularizing a practice previously confined to folk tradition or elite curiosity. His work fundamentally transformed the tarot from a game or simple oracle into a structured esoteric tool, establishing the foundational concepts for modern occult tarot interpretation and influencing subsequent generations of mystics and diviners across Western Europe.

Etteilla's seminal contribution began with his 1781 work, 'Manière de tirer les cartes' (How to Draw the Cards), which laid out specific divinatory meanings for each of the 78 tarot cards, including reversals. He claimed these interpretations were derived from ancient Egyptian sources, specifically the 'Book of Thoth', a popular but historically unfounded occult theory of the era. From 1783 to 1785, he published his 'Enseignement théorique et pratique du Livre de Thoth' (Theoretical and Practical Instruction of the Book of Thoth), detailing his unique deck design and reading methods. Etteilla further established himself as the first known professional tarot reader, operating a successful divination practice in Paris and making his living solely through cartomancy, thereby creating a new occult profession.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Etteilla pioneered the systematic interpretation of tarot for divination, professionalizing the practice and influencing generations of occultists and the popular understanding of tarot's origins. His work transformed a game into a widespread esoteric tool, selling thousands of books and decks.
